title: Active and Passive Voice
shortDescription: Same action, different camera angle — a tense-by-tense conversion guide instead of one paragraph trying to cover all twelve tenses at once.
genZNote: Active puts the doer in the spotlight. Passive turns the camera around to focus on who got acted upon instead.

sections.heading: Core concept
sections.body: In the ACTIVE voice, the subject performs the action: 'The chef COOKED the meal.' In the PASSIVE voice, the subject receives the action, and the doer becomes optional (often introduced by 'by'): 'The meal WAS COOKED (by the chef).' The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence, and the original subject either moves into a 'by' phrase or is dropped entirely if unimportant or unknown.

sections.heading: Passive voice formula by tense (subject + form of 'be' + past participle)

rows: A letter is written by him.
A letter is being written by him.
A letter has been written by him.
A letter was written by him.
A letter was being written by him.
A letter had been written by him.
A letter will be written by him.
A letter can be written by him.

sections.heading: Special conversion cases
bullets: Questions: 'Did he write the letter?' → 'Was the letter written by him?' — the auxiliary still moves to the front.
Imperatives/commands: 'Close the door' → 'Let the door be closed.'
Sentences with two objects (indirect + direct): 'He gave her a book' can become either 'She was given a book (by him)' or 'A book was given to her (by him)' — both are valid passive forms.
Sentences with a modal + 'have': 'He must have finished the work' → 'The work must have been finished (by him).'

sections.heading: When passive voice is genuinely useful vs a trap
bullets: Passive voice is preferred when the DOER is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately vague: 'The window was broken' (we don't know/care who).
Passive voice is preferred in formal/scientific writing to keep focus on the process: 'The solution was heated to 60°C.'

Passive voice is usually a weaker STYLE choice (not a grammar error) when the doer is known and important — exams sometimes ask you to recognise that a sentence would read better in active voice, which is a style judgement, not a hard rule.
Intransitive verbs (verbs with no object — sleep, arrive, happen) CANNOT be converted to passive voice at all, since there's no object to promote to subject.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Passive voice moves the object of an active sentence into the subject position, using the correct tense of 'be' plus the past participle, with the original doer optional in a 'by' phrase.
keyFacts: The passive formula is always: subject (was the object) + correct form of 'be' + past participle (+ by + doer).
Questions keep the auxiliary at the front even after converting to passive.
Intransitive verbs (no object) cannot be made passive.

highYieldFacts: The tense of the passive sentence must match the tense of the original active sentence exactly — only the 'be' form and word order change.
An intransitive verb like 'arrive' or 'happen' has no passive form.
commonTraps: Getting the past participle wrong for irregular verbs (write → written, not writed).
Forgetting to shift the auxiliary to the front when converting a question to passive.
Trying to passivise an intransitive verb.
mustRemember: Identify the tense of the active sentence FIRST, then apply that tense's specific passive formula.
possibleQuestions: Convert to passive voice: 'They are building a new bridge.'
Convert to passive voice: 'Who broke the window?'
